title: I Am Providence: the Angell Street House, the Amateur Press, and the Return from Brooklyn
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: 454 Angell Street, Providence: the birth at nine in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; hplovecraft.com's chronology and the birth certificate give 20 August 1890, 9 a.m. The address is given by hplovecraft.com as 454 (then numbered 194) Angell Street; the house no longer stands and the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for 454 Angell Street, out toward Wayland Square, not the College Hill point the research dossier first carried.
stops.campa: At nine in the morning, in her father's house on Angell Street, Sarah Susan Phillips Lovecraft gives birth to her only child. The house belongs to Whipple Van Buren Phillips: industrialist, dam builder, speculator in Idaho land, owner of the library the boy will be turned loose in. It does not outlast the boy. Howard Phillips Lovecraft will pass nearly the whole of his life within a mile of this doorstep. His father, Winfield Scott Lovecraft, sells silver for Gorham and Company of Providence and is on the road more than he is home.
sources: hplovecraft.com, biographical chronology and Life/Documents (birth certificate)
Nominatim geocode, 454 Angell Street, Wayland, Providence
suggested_refs: The Phillips house at 454 Angell Street, demolished; photographs held with the Lovecraft collection at Brown

stops.name: Butler Hospital, Providence: the salesman brought back from Chicago
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested from the Butler Hospital admission record as cited by Wikipedia; the day is defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for Butler Hospital, 345 Blackstone Boulevard.
stops.campa: Winfield Scott Lovecraft, traveling for the silversmiths, collapses in a Chicago hotel and is brought east raving. Butler Hospital takes him onto its Blackstone Boulevard grounds, a private asylum for families who can pay, and he never leaves it again. His son is two and a half years old. In the household on Angell Street the father is spoken of as paralyzed, an invalid on a long convalescence in a distant institution. Whether the child ever learned what the doctors had written down is not recoverable from anything he left behind.
sources: Wikipedia, 'H. P. Lovecraft', citing the Butler Hospital admission record
suggested_refs: Butler Hospital admission and case records, Providence, 1893-1898

stops.name: Butler Hospital, Providence: general paresis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; hplovecraft.com and Wikipedia both give 19 July 1898, citing the Butler Hospital death record. The reading of general paresis as tertiary neurosyphilis is the standard clinical translation, not a separate document.
stops.campa: Five years and three months after his admission, Winfield Scott Lovecraft dies in the asylum. The death record gives general paresis, which in 1898 means the last stage of syphilis, which means the collapse in Chicago was the end of something contracted before his son was born. Howard is one month short of eight. His grandmother Robie Alzada Place Phillips had died two years earlier, and to that first death the boy answered in verse: The Poem of Ulysses, made at six or seven, is the earliest writing of his that anyone kept.
sources: Wikipedia, 'H. P. Lovecraft', citing the Butler Hospital death record
suggested_refs: The Poem of Ulysses (1897), earliest surviving juvenile manuscript

stops.name: 454 Angell Street, Providence: The Rhode Island Journal of Astronomy
stops.date_confidence: year corrected from the dossier's 1902 to 1903 and month and day defaulted to 01. Open Library full text gives the run as 1903-1907 and Lovecraft's own account as 'in 1903 astronomy became my...'; Wikipedia's 1902 refers to astronomy taking hold of his worldview, a separate statement the dossier had conflated with the founding of the periodical.
stops.campa: Astronomy takes the boy the way religion takes other children. He keeps a telescope on the back lot, learns the sky by heart, and begins issuing a paper of his own out of the house: The Rhode Island Journal of Astronomy, made by pencil, pen and hectograph, addressed to a readership of relatives and two or three schoolfellows. In 1906 the Providence Sunday Journal prints a letter from him on an astronomical question, the first of his writing to appear in a paper he did not manufacture himself. The hectographed journal itself runs until 1907.
sources: Open Library full-text search, The Rhode Island Journal of Astronomy (1903-07)
suggested_refs: Surviving hectographed issues of The Rhode Island Journal of Astronomy, John Hay Library

stops.name: 598 Angell Street, Providence: the smaller house
stops.date_confidence: year attested by hplovecraft.com and Wikipedia; month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for 598 Angell Street, which places the duplex further east than the dossier's College Hill point, away from Brown rather than toward it.
stops.campa: Whipple Phillips's ventures fail, in Idaho and elsewhere, and the old man dies in the wreck of them. The estate cannot carry the Angell Street house. Lovecraft and his mother move into half a duplex further out the same street: no grounds, no servants, no library. For the rest of his life he will describe the move as a fall out of a station he was born into, and he counts the address itself among the things taken from him. Angell Street it still is, at a number he can afford. He is fourteen years old.
sources: Nominatim geocode, 598 Angell Street, Wayland, Providence
suggested_refs: Probate and business records of Whipple Van Buren Phillips, Providence, 1904

stops.name: Hope Street High School, Providence: the diploma not taken
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the collapse and the end of his schooling; month and day defaulted to 01. Wikipedia notes the medical character of the 1908 breakdown is undocumented, and later claims of a suicide attempt are unsupported. The present Hope High School building dates from 1938; the coordinate marks the site, not the structure he attended.
stops.campa: He attends intermittently, strong in chemistry, astronomy and history, defeated by mathematics, absent for long stretches with complaints nobody names precisely. In 1908 something gives way and he simply stops going. He leaves without a diploma, and Brown University, a mile from his door and full of the astronomers he has been writing to, is closed to him for good. What the breakdown consisted of no medical record says. He is seventeen and he goes home to his mother.
stops.quote: I am only about half alive - a large part of my strength is consumed in sitting up or walking.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Alfred Galpin, 27 May 1918, quoted at en.wikiquote.org/wiki/H._P._Lovecraft
sources: Nominatim geocode, Hope High School, 324 Hope Street
suggested_refs: Hope Street High School attendance registers, Providence Public Schools, 1904-1908

stops.name: Providence Athenaeum, Benefit Street: the reading
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Athenaeum habit is standard in Providence Lovecraft topography (Beckwith, Lovecraft's Providence and Adjacent Parts) but no dated visit was confirmed in the sources reached for this file; the date only orders the segment. Poe's standing as his earliest decisive influence, discovered around age eight, comes from the research dossier rather than a document fetched here, though Supernatural Horror in Literature makes the debt plain in his own hand.
stops.campa: On Benefit Street, in the granite subscription library where the city keeps its older books, the shut-in reads. Poe first and hardest, taken at eight and never put down. Then the Gothic novelists, the eighteenth century essayists whose prose he adopts wholesale as his own, the astronomers, the chemists. Supernatural Horror in Literature, written two decades later, is assembled largely out of these shelves and his memory. Between 1908 and 1913 he publishes almost nothing and sees almost nobody.
stops.quote: The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Lovecraft, Supernatural Horror in Literature, opening sentence (written 1925-27, first serialized 1927)
sources: hplovecraft.com, texts of Supernatural Horror in Literature
Beckwith, Lovecraft's Providence and Adjacent Parts, as cited in the research dossier
suggested_refs: The Providence Athenaeum, 251 Benefit Street
Supernatural Horror in Literature (1927), his account of the Poe inheritance

stops.name: 598 Angell Street, Providence: the letter against Fred Jackson
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day defaulted to 01. The verse feud ran through the following year in the Argosy letters column.
stops.campa: He is twenty-three and has published nothing that pays when he sends Argosy a letter denouncing the romance writer Fred Jackson, whose serials he finds insipid past bearing. The letters column answers back, at length, and for a year Lovecraft conducts a public war in heroic couplets against Jackson's defenders. It is the first sustained contact he has had with anyone outside his mother's house in five years. Among the readers of the column is Edward F. Daas, an officer of the United Amateur Press Association. The couplets are doggerel and Lovecraft enjoys writing them enormously.
suggested_refs: The Argosy letters columns, 1913-1914, and Lovecraft's verse contributions to the Jackson controversy

stops.name: 598 Angell Street, Providence: the invitation from Edward F. Daas
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested by Wikipedia and hplovecraft.com; day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Daas, an officer of the United Amateur Press Association, writes to the man conducting a poetic feud in a pulp magazine's letters column and asks him to join. Lovecraft joins in April. Amateur journalism is a national network of hobbyists who print their own papers on their own presses and post them to each other for criticism; it costs almost nothing, it demands writing, and it supplies correspondents by the hundred. He had applied to nothing and asked no one. The invitation arrives in the post at 598 Angell Street.
suggested_refs: United Amateur Press Association membership rolls and journals, 1914-1923

stops.name: 598 Angell Street, Providence: The Conservative, The Alchemist, Dagon
stops.date_confidence: the stop gathers four attested events across 1915-1918 at one address: The Conservative begun 1915 (thirteen issues to 1923), The Alchemist published 1916, Dagon written 1917, the UAPA presidency 1917-1918. The date is set at 1916 to order the segment; month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He edits a paper of his own, The Conservative, thirteen issues over eight years, filled with reactionary politics, metrical orthodoxy and campaigns against free verse. In 1916 an amateur journal prints The Alchemist, written at eighteen: his first published story. In 1917 he writes Dagon, in which a castaway on a risen seafloor sees something come up out of the water to embrace a monolith, and the pulpit oratory falls away from the prose. He serves as president of the association in 1917 and again in 1918.
stops.quote: My present opinions waver betwixt Pantheism and rationalism. I am a sort of agnostic, neither affirming nor denying anything.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Maurice W. Moe, 16 January 1915, Selected Letters I, ed. Derleth and Wandrei, p. 10
suggested_refs: The Conservative, thirteen issues, 1915-1923
The Vagrant (1919), first printing of Dagon

stops.name: Boston: Lord Dunsany at the lectern
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the research dossier's chronology and consistent with standard biographical accounts (Joshi, I Am Providence); the exact hall was not confirmed in the sources fetched, so the coordinate marks central Boston and the month and day are defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Dunsany comes to Boston to lecture and Lovecraft travels up to see him: an Irish peer who invented a pantheon of his own and wrote it in the cadence of the King James Bible. From that evening Lovecraft takes a licence rather than a technique: a writer may invent the gods, and invent the books that describe them. The imitation of the manner lasts years, as he himself later admits. He begins making dream countries with names out of nowhere, Sarnath and Ulthar and unknown Kadath, and for a while every sentence he writes has the King James roll in it.
stops.quote: There is a real restfulness in the scientific conviction that nothing matters very much; that the only legitimate aim of humanity is to minimise acute suffering for the majority, and to derive whatever satisfaction is derivable from the exercise of the mind in the pursuit of truth.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Reinhardt Kleiner, 14 September 1919, Selected Letters I, pp. 86-87
sources: Research dossier chronology, cross-checked against Wikipedia, 'H. P. Lovecraft'
suggested_refs: Lord Dunsany's 1919 American lecture tour
The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath and the Dunsanian tales, 1919-1927

stops.name: Butler Hospital, Providence: the mother in her turn
stops.date_confidence: month and year of admission attested from the Butler Hospital record as cited by Wikipedia; day defaulted to 01. Her death on 24 May 1921 following gallbladder surgery is attested by hplovecraft.com and Wikipedia. No modern diagnosis can be established from the surviving record.
stops.campa: Sarah Susan Phillips Lovecraft, after years of depression, anxiety and somatic complaint, is admitted in March to the institution that held her husband until it buried him. Mother and son do not meet again; for two years they write letters across four miles of the same city. On 24 May 1921 she dies there after gallbladder surgery. What was actually wrong with her cannot be established from what survives. He is thirty years old. The letters between the two houses stop in May.
stops.quote: It is good to be a cynic - it is better to be a contented cat - and it is best not to exist at all.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Lovecraft, Nietzscheism and Realism, The Rainbow I.1 (October 1921); Collected Essays 5, ed. Joshi, p. 71
sources: Wikipedia, 'H. P. Lovecraft', citing the Butler Hospital admission record
Collected Essays, Volume 5: Philosophy, ed. S. T. Joshi
suggested_refs: The Lovecraft-Susan Lovecraft correspondence, 1919-1921, John Hay Library

stops.name: Boston: the amateur convention and Sonia Haft Greene
stops.date_confidence: hplovecraft.com's chronology gives 4 July 1921 and Wikipedia gives July 1921; the day is taken from hplovecraft.com. The convention hall was not identified in sources fetched, so the coordinate marks central Boston.
stops.campa: Six weeks after his mother's funeral he goes up to an amateur journalism convention in Boston and is introduced to Sonia Haft Greene: born in Ukraine, Jewish, seven years his senior, a milliner earning good money in a Manhattan hat shop, an organizer in the amateur press, and not at all frightened of him. She takes him to dinner, and the aunts in Providence hear nothing about it. The correspondence begins that week, then visits, then trips to Magnolia and Newport.
suggested_refs: Sonia H. Davis, The Private Life of H. P. Lovecraft (memoir)

stops.name: Marblehead, Massachusetts: ten past four in the afternoon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and nearly to the minute; Wikipedia's article on Kingsport documents the first sight of Marblehead on 17 December 1922 at about 4.05 to 4.10 p.m. The research dossier had dated the first visit 1926-1930, four years late, while carrying the superlative that belongs to this afternoon.
stops.campa: He comes over from Salem on a December afternoon and climbs into the old town as the light goes: colonial roofs stacked up a rock above a harbor, gables and chimneys unaltered since 1700, the whole seaport gray and steep and still. He is thirty-two years old. Out of that afternoon he builds Kingsport, and for years he comes back to the real streets to keep the invented ones accurate. The Festival, written the next year, walks a narrator up these same lanes at Christmas. He fixes the hour at about ten past four.
stops.quote: the most powerful single emotional climax during my nearly forty years of existence
stops.quote_source: Lovecraft on his first sight of Marblehead, 17 December 1922, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Kingsport (Lovecraft)'
suggested_refs: Old Town, Marblehead, from which Kingsport is drawn
The Festival (1923) and The Strange High House in the Mist (1926)

stops.name: 598 Angell Street, Providence: Weird Tales takes five stories
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for the magazine's launch and Edwin Baird's acceptances; month and day defaulted to 01. The stop is pinned at Lovecraft's own Providence address rather than the magazine's Chicago office, which he never visited.
stops.campa: A new pulp appears out of Chicago given over entirely to the strange, and its first editor, Edwin Baird, buys five of the stories Lovecraft sends him, Dagon and The Rats in the Walls among them. This is the beginning of a professional career that never once supports him. He is paid on publication, sometimes at a cent a word, sometimes late, sometimes not at all, and he props up the income by revising other men's manuscripts for a fee. The magazine prints him for fourteen years.
stops.quote: Only a cynic can create horror—for behind every masterpiece of the sort must reside a driving daemonic force that despises the human race and its illusions, and longs to pull them to pieces and mock them.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Edwin Baird, printed in Weird Tales 3, no. 3 (March 1924), pp. 89-92; reprinted in Lord of a Visible World, ed. S. T. Joshi, p. 122
sources: Lord of a Visible World, ed. S. T. Joshi
suggested_refs: Weird Tales, vols. 1-30 (1923-1937), the run in which most of his fiction first appeared

stops.name: St. Paul's Chapel, Manhattan: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the marriage certificate reproduced at hplovecraft.com and by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: They marry at St. Paul's Chapel on Broadway, the oldest church still standing in Manhattan, and nobody in Providence is told beforehand. Sonia is thirty-eight, Lovecraft thirty-three. He has never lived anywhere but his family's houses, and he has no income of his own; his wife has one. They will live under one roof for less than a year. The letter announcing the fact reaches his aunts Lillian Clark and Annie Gamwell after the ceremony, which is how he intended it.
suggested_refs: The marriage certificate of Howard P. Lovecraft and Sonia H. Greene, 3 March 1924

stops.name: 259 Parkside Avenue, Brooklyn: the Kalem Club
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia for the couple's residence at 259 Parkside Avenue; the month is set to April purely to order the stop after the March wedding, and the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The flat faces Prospect Park, and for one season New York is the finest antiquarian playground he has ever been handed: Dutch farmhouses out in Flatbush, colonial burying grounds, museum collections, and all-night walks with a circle of writers who call themselves the Kalem Club after the initials of their names. He is talkative, sociable, almost happy. Sonia's hat business fails that same year, her health goes with it, and the income that was supposed to carry the household stops coming in.
suggested_refs: The Kalem Club circle: Frank Belknap Long, Samuel Loveman, Rheinhart Kleiner, George Kirk

stops.name: Brooklyn: the pit under the Sphinx, signed by Houdini
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. The ghostwriting itself is standard in the Lovecraft bibliographies reflected on hplovecraft.com but the dossier tags it [R]; the year 1924 is attested for the commission and publication, while the month is set only to order the stop within it.
stops.campa: Weird Tales hands him a commission: a first-person adventure to run over Harry Houdini's name, in which the escape artist is bound, lowered into a pit beneath the Sphinx, and learns what is kept down there. Lovecraft throws out most of the premise and writes it as his own. It appears as Imprisoned with the Pharaohs, by Houdini, and the magazine pays better for another man's byline than it has ever paid for his. He does this kind of work, uncredited and for a flat fee, for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Imprisoned with the Pharaohs, Weird Tales, May-June-July 1924, published as by Harry Houdini

stops.name: 169 Clinton Street, Brooklyn Heights: the single room
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: hplovecraft.com gives 1 January 1925 for the move. Coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for 169 Clinton Street, which is in Brooklyn Heights; the dossier's surrounding text had blurred this address into Red Hook, and Wikipedia's own account keeps them distinct.
stops.campa: Sonia takes work in Cleveland and the marriage becomes an arrangement conducted by post. Lovecraft moves alone into one room on Clinton Street, cheaper than the Parkside flat, and lives on tinned beans and cheese to hold the rent. In May his suit and his clothes are stolen out of the room. The letters he writes from this address are the ugliest documents of his life: page after page on the immigrant crowds in the streets below, set down by a man who has himself become an unemployable foreigner in a city that will not have him.
sources: Nominatim geocode, 169 Clinton Street, Brooklyn Heights
suggested_refs: Selected Letters I-II, the Brooklyn letters of 1925-1926

stops.name: Red Hook, Brooklyn: the waterfront district
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia as the setting and year of The Horror at Red Hook; the month is set only to order the stop, and the record shows Red Hook as a district within walking distance of his room rather than a dated single visit.
stops.campa: A walk south of his room, the waterfront takes in the ships and the people who come off them, packed into old brick by the thousand. Lovecraft walks there and hates what he sees, and out of the hatred comes The Horror at Red Hook, in which immigrant tenements front for a cult older than Europe. He knows the story is bad and says so. The prejudice his letters record in private is on the printed page here, undisguised, over his own name in Weird Tales for January 1927.
suggested_refs: The Horror at Red Hook, Weird Tales, January 1927
He (1926), the companion New York story

stops.name: 10 Barnes Street, Providence: the return
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by hplovecraft.com's chronology. Coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for 10-12 Barnes Street, College Hill, about 200 metres from the point the dossier carried.
stops.campa: His aunts find him rooms on Barnes Street and he comes home, two years and six weeks after the wedding, to a colonial doorway on College Hill and a fireplace of his own. The exile is finished. In the weeks before the move he writes to Lillian Clark about what the city is to him, and the sentence he ends on will be cut into his gravestone forty years later. In the first eighteen months back he produces The Call of Cthulhu, The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, The Case of Charles Dexter Ward and The Colour Out of Space.
stops.quote: Providence is part of me - I am Providence.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Lillian D. Clark, 29 March 1926, quoted at en.wikiquote.org/wiki/H._P._Lovecraft
sources: Nominatim geocode, 10-12 Barnes Street, College Hill, Providence
suggested_refs: 10 Barnes Street, Providence, standing
Letters to Lillian D. Clark, 1924-1926

stops.name: 10 Barnes Street, Providence: The Call of Cthulhu
stops.date_confidence: year of composition attested (1926) by hplovecraft.com; the month is set to order the stop after the April return, and the day is defaulted to 01. First publication in Weird Tales, February 1928.
stops.campa: In the summer after his return he writes the story that names the whole apparatus. A dead Providence professor's papers, a sculptor's dreams, a police raid on a cult in the Louisiana swamps, the log of a Norwegian sailor: four documents that mean nothing separately and, laid side by side by a narrator who wishes he had left them alone, disclose a thing asleep under the Pacific and the men who wait for it to wake. Weird Tales buys the story and holds it in a drawer until 1928.
stops.quote: The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Lovecraft, The Call of Cthulhu (1926), opening sentence
sources: hplovecraft.com, text of The Call of Cthulhu and bibliographic chronology
suggested_refs: The Call of Cthulhu, Weird Tales, February 1928

stops.name: 10 Barnes Street, Providence: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward
stops.date_confidence: year of composition attested (1927) by hplovecraft.com; month and day defaulted to 01. The novel was never submitted for publication in his lifetime and appeared only after his death.
stops.campa: He writes a novel and submits it nowhere. A Providence antiquarian, working from an ancestor's papers, raises the ancestor out of his essential salts and is quietly replaced by him. The streets are Lovecraft's own streets, named as they stand, and the eighteenth century Providence in the book is assembled out of deeds, directories and doorways he passes every day of his life. The typescript stays in a drawer. Weird Tales prints it, cut, four years after he is dead.
stops.quote: I say to you againe, doe not call up Any that you can not put downe; by the Which I meane, Any that can in Turne call up somewhat against you, whereby your Powerfullest Devices may not be of use.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Lovecraft, The Case of Charles Dexter Ward (1927), Jedediah Orne to Joseph Curwen
sources: hplovecraft.com, text of The Case of Charles Dexter Ward and bibliographic chronology
suggested_refs: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, first published (abridged) in Weird Tales, May and July 1941

stops.name: 10 Barnes Street, Providence: the papers signed in Cleveland
stops.date_confidence: year attested by hplovecraft.com, which lists the 1929 divorce; month and day defaulted to 01. Whether the decree was ever finalized is unresolved in the documentary record, since Lovecraft appears never to have completed the final step, and the stop is pinned at his own address rather than at Sonia's in Cleveland.
stops.campa: Sonia sends the papers and signs them in 1929. Lovecraft appears never to have completed the decree, so whether the marriage legally ended at all is a question the surviving record does not answer. He is thirty-eight, back in his aunt's orbit, and the writing life reorganizes itself around the post: letters to Clark Ashton Smith in California, to Robert E. Howard in Texas, to Frank Belknap Long, to schoolboys who write him fan mail and get four pages back by return. Most of his working hours go into envelopes.
stops.quote: I love to dream, but I never try to dream and think at the same time.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Woodburn Harris, 25 February to 1 March 1929, quoted at en.wikiquote.org/wiki/H._P._Lovecraft
sources: Research dossier synthesis of Joshi-derived accounts
suggested_refs: Selected Letters II-III (1925-1931)

stops.name: Salem, Massachusetts: the witch city and the making of Arkham
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. Salem is attested as a repeated destination through the 1920s in the dossier's destination list and is consistent with Wikipedia's account of his New England travel, but no dated visit was confirmed in sources fetched; the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Salem is an hour away and he goes back and back: gambrel roofs, the House of the Seven Gables, and a documented history of judicial murder within the memory of the town's own deeds. Out of it he takes Arkham, the invented Massachusetts city where his professors and his witch-cults live. He travels the cheapest way a man can travel, sitting up in buses through the night, eating cold beans out of a tin in his coat pocket so the fare will stretch to one more town.
stops.quote: I should describe mine own nature as tripartite, my interests consisting of three parallel and dissociated groups - (a) Love of the strange and fantastic. (b) Love of the abstract truth and of scientific logick. (c) Love of the ancient and the permanent.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Reinhardt Kleiner, 7 March 1920, Selected Letters I, p. 110
suggested_refs: The Salem witch trial records, from which the Arkham material is drawn

stops.name: Charleston, South Carolina: An Account of Charleston
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia and the dossier's works list for the visit and the resulting essay; the month is set within the attested spring-summer 1930 travel season to order the segment, and the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The 1930 season carries him further south than he has ever been. Charleston keeps its colonial and antebellum streets nearly whole, and he walks them for days. He never sets a tale here. What he wants from the South is architectural: ironwork, fanlights, brick laid before the Revolution, a street plan older than the Republic. The account he writes runs longer than most of his stories and reads like a gazetteer composed by a man in love, and he titles it An Account of Charleston in His Majesty's Province of South-Carolina.
suggested_refs: H. P. Lovecraft, An Account of Charleston in His Majesty's Province of South-Carolina (1930)

stops.name: Brattleboro, Vermont: the hill country
stops.date_confidence: attested by Wikipedia as a stop on the spring-summer 1930 circuit; the month is set within that season to order the segment, and the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He passes through Brattleboro on the 1930 circuit, up in the Vermont hill country where the farms sit in folded valleys and the roads run out. Two years earlier he had put that landscape into The Whisperer in Darkness, with its flooded rivers washing unnameable bodies down out of the hills. He stays with correspondents, walks, and moves on. The itinerary of that summer runs Charleston, Vermont, western Massachusetts and Quebec, all of it done on bus fare and other people's spare rooms.
suggested_refs: The Whisperer in Darkness (1930), set in the Vermont hill country

stops.name: Quebec City: the walled town
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia and by the dossier's works list; the month is set within the 1930 travel season to order the segment, and the day is defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The one foreign country he ever reaches is Quebec, and it undoes him: a walled town on a rock, French, Catholic, seventeenth century in its bones, with ramparts and a citadel and streets that have never been straightened. He goes back three times in the last seven years of his life. What comes out of the first visit is A Description of the Town of Quebeck, in New-France, one hundred and thirty-six pages in longhand, the longest thing he ever wrote about anything.
suggested_refs: H. P. Lovecraft, A Description of the Town of Quebeck, in New-France (1930-31), his longest single work

stops.name: St. Augustine, Florida: the Spanish fort
stops.date_confidence: year attested only by the dated travel essay itself in the consulted bibliography; a separate biographical page confirming the visit was not located, and the month is set to order the segment with the day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The oldest continuously occupied European town in the country, and he walks it with the same notebook: the coquina fort, the Spanish street plan, the gates. He writes it up as A Visit to St. Augustine. In March he had finished a novel about a dead city in the Antarctic. Cold below about forty degrees can drop him unconscious in the street, and has more than once, so Florida suits him as no place further north does. He is forty years old and travelling on bus fare.
sources: Research dossier works list, A Visit to St. Augustine (1931)
suggested_refs: H. P. Lovecraft, A Visit to St. Augustine (1931)

stops.name: 10 Barnes Street, Providence: At the Mountains of Madness refused
stops.date_confidence: year of composition and rejection attested (1931) by hplovecraft.com and Wikipedia; the month is set to order the stop and the day is defaulted to 01. Serialized by Astounding Stories in 1936.
stops.campa: He finishes a short novel: an Antarctic expedition finds a mountain range higher than the Himalayas, and behind it a city built by things that came to this planet before there was anything alive on it to see them arrive. Farnsworth Wright at Weird Tales reads it and says no: too long, too slow. He writes much less afterward, submits less, and tells his correspondents he is finished as a writer. Astounding Stories prints it in 1936, cut and misprinted.
suggested_refs: At the Mountains of Madness, Astounding Stories, February to April 1936

stops.name: Newburyport, Massachusetts: the model for Innsmouth
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's article on The Shadow over Innsmouth states without hedge that Lovecraft based Innsmouth on his impressions of Newburyport, visited in 1923 and in the fall of 1931; the dossier had carried this as an unattributed fan tradition. The month is set within the attested fall 1931 window, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He has seen Newburyport once before, in 1923, and comes back in the fall of 1931. In November and December, straight out of the visit, he writes The Shadow over Innsmouth: a town whose people made a bargain with something in the sea and have been paying it out in their own faces for three generations. The novella never names Newburyport. The port he walks through is decayed, half its houses shut, the shipping gone elsewhere, the money that built the Federal mansions a century out of date.
suggested_refs: The Shadow over Innsmouth (written November-December 1931)

stops.name: 66 College Street, Providence: the last address
stops.date_confidence: year attested by hplovecraft.com and Wikipedia; month and day defaulted to 01. Aunt Lillian Clark's death in 1932 is attested by hplovecraft.com. The address is a live discrepancy in the sources: hplovecraft.com gives 66 College Street, Wikipedia gives 66 Prospect Street. The Klinger and De Camp volumes resolve it in favor of College Street and explain Wikipedia's error, since the house was physically moved in 1959 and renumbered 65 Prospect Street. The coordinate is the original College Street site.
stops.campa: Aunt Lillian Clark dies in 1932, and what is left of the family money will not keep two households. Lovecraft and his surviving aunt, Annie Gamwell, move into a small rear apartment in a wooden house of 1825, up against the Brown University campus, with a view of a colonial garden. He is poorer here than he has ever been and the address delights him: old woodwork and a garden, on the exact ground he was born to. He writes The Thing on the Doorstep in this room.
sources: Wikipedia, 'H. P. Lovecraft' (which gives the address as 66 Prospect Street)
The New Annotated H. P. Lovecraft, ed. Klinger
L. Sprague de Camp, H. P. Lovecraft: A Biography
suggested_refs: The Samuel B. Mumford House, built 1825 at 66 College Street

stops.name: DeLand, Florida: the boy who kept the papers
stops.date_confidence: visits attested for 1934 and 1935 in the dossier chronology, consistent with hplovecraft.com's account of Barlow's later custody of the papers; the month is set to order the stop, the day defaulted to 01, and the coordinate marks the town centre since the Barlow homestead's exact location was not confirmed.
stops.campa: R. H. Barlow is sixteen when the correspondence starts, and Lovecraft goes down to Florida twice to stay with his family, weeks at a time. The boy collects: he keeps the letters, the drafts, the discarded pages nobody else thinks worth a shelf. Before he leaves, Lovecraft writes out an instruction naming Barlow to take charge of his papers if he dies. The weeks go in revising manuscripts on the porch, canoeing, feeding the cats, with a sixteen-year-old reading over his shoulder.
suggested_refs: Instructions in Case of Decease (1936), naming Barlow custodian of the papers

stops.name: 66 College Street, Providence: The Shadow Out of Time
stops.date_confidence: composition attested to 1934-1935 by hplovecraft.com's bibliographic chronology; the later year is taken and month and day defaulted to 01. Published in Astounding Stories, 1936.
stops.campa: A professor of political economy at Miskatonic University blacks out in 1908 and wakes five years later with no memory of what walked around in his body meanwhile. What walked around in it was a mind from a species that ruled the earth a hundred and fifty million years ago and keeps its records in a library under the Australian desert, where he eventually finds a volume written in his own handwriting. Lovecraft rewrites the story three times and thinks it a failure.
suggested_refs: The Shadow Out of Time, Astounding Stories, June 1936

stops.name: 66 College Street, Providence: the only book
stops.date_confidence: year attested; hplovecraft.com notes the 1936 book publication and the standard bibliographic record gives about 400 copies printed with roughly 200 bound. Month and day defaulted to 01. The stop is pinned at Lovecraft's own address, not at the Everett, Pennsylvania premises of Visionary Publishing Co., which he never visited.
stops.campa: William Crawford, an amateur publisher in Pennsylvania, sets The Shadow over Innsmouth in hard covers: about four hundred copies printed, perhaps two hundred ever bound, the text carrying enough errors to make the author wince for the rest of his life. It is the only book of his fiction published while he is alive. He has been writing for thirty years and is forty-five. The firm is Visionary Publishing Co. of Everett, Pennsylvania, and he never sees the premises.
sources: Research dossier synthesis of the standard bibliographic record
suggested_refs: The Shadow over Innsmouth, Visionary Publishing Co., Everett, Pennsylvania, 1936

stops.name: 66 College Street, Providence: In Memoriam, Robert Ervin Howard
stops.date_confidence: Howard's death on 11 June 1936 is attested in the standard biographical record reflected in Wikipedia's H. P. Lovecraft article; the stop is dated to that day and pinned at Lovecraft's own address in Providence, since Howard died in Cross Plains, Texas, and Lovecraft was never there.
stops.campa: The news comes by letter from Texas: Robert E. Howard, six years his correspondent and never once his acquaintance in the flesh, has shot himself at thirty on the morning his mother was dying. Lovecraft writes an obituary for the amateur press, In Memoriam: Robert Ervin Howard, and tells everyone who will listen that the loss to the field is irreparable. For six years the two of them had argued on paper about barbarism and civilization, the frontier against the antiquarian's city. Neither had persuaded the other.
sources: Research dossier synthesis of the standard biographical record
suggested_refs: H. P. Lovecraft, In Memoriam: Robert Ervin Howard (1936)
The Lovecraft-Howard correspondence, 1930-1936

stops.name: 66 College Street, Providence: the doctor sent for at last
stops.date_confidence: month and year attested in the Joshi-derived accounts the dossier summarizes; day defaulted to 01. The physician's name is corrected here: the dossier's 'Dr. Cecil B. Leet' returns zero hits in Open Library's entire scanned corpus and appears to be fabricated. The New Annotated H. P. Lovecraft and Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos both name Dr. Cecil Calvert Dustin, an internal medicine doctor. hplovecraft.com's chronology names no physician at all.
stops.campa: He has had abdominal pain for months and has not gone to anyone about it, partly from stoicism and partly because there is no money. In February Dr. Cecil Calvert Dustin examines him and finds cancer of the intestine, well past operating. There is no operation to be had and no money for one. Lovecraft goes home and keeps a notebook of his symptoms in the same hand he used for his commonplace book: the temperature, the pain, the hours. He goes on answering letters while he keeps it.
sources: The New Annotated H. P. Lovecraft, ed. Klinger (naming Dr. Cecil Calvert Dustin)
Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (same identification)
suggested_refs: Lovecraft's final clinical notebook, sometimes called the death diary, John Hay Library

stops.name: Jane Brown Memorial Hospital, Providence: admitted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by hplovecraft.com and Wikipedia. Jane Brown Memorial was a unit of Rhode Island Hospital; the coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for Rhode Island Hospital, 593 Eddy Street, about 600 metres from the point the dossier carried.
stops.campa: He is taken across town to the hospital on the tenth of March, having stayed in the College Street apartment as long as Annie Gamwell can manage him there. She is the last of his aunts and the last of the household. The notebook of symptoms he has kept since February ends before the admission. He is forty-six years old and he weighs very little. The record of these five days is thin: he is in pain, he is given whatever 1937 has to give against pain, and he goes on asking about his mail.
sources: Nominatim geocode, Rhode Island Hospital, 593 Eddy Street
suggested_refs: Jane Brown Memorial Hospital, a unit of Rhode Island Hospital, Providence

stops.name: Jane Brown Memorial Hospital, Providence: a quarter past seven in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the minute; the death certificate reproduced at hplovecraft.com gives 7.15 a.m., 15 March 1937, carcinoma of the small intestine with chronic nephritis contributory.
stops.campa: He dies at a quarter past seven on a Monday morning, five days after admission, of carcinoma of the small intestine, with chronic nephritis named on the certificate as contributing. He is forty-six years old. He leaves an estate of essentially nothing, one badly printed book, and some sixty stories scattered through pulp magazines. The bulk of what survives him is correspondence, tens of thousands of letters by estimate, sitting in other people's houses, and nobody has ever counted them.
suggested_refs: Death certificate of Howard P. Lovecraft, Providence, 15 March 1937

stops.name: 187 Benefit Street, Providence: the funeral at Knowles' Sons
stops.date_confidence: date attested by hplovecraft.com. The address was located for this file in the 1937 and 1938 Providence city directories via Open Library full-text search: Horace B. Knowles' Sons Inc., established 1854, 187 Benefit Street, an earlier directory giving 188. The dossier had marked the location unconfirmed and used a placeholder coordinate about 640 metres away.
stops.campa: The funeral is held at Horace B. Knowles' Sons, undertakers on Benefit Street since 1854. The attendance is small, and the Providence papers give the death a modest notice, which is one of the roots of the later belief that he died wholly unread; in fact he is read, in the pulps, by people who will spend the next forty years putting him into hardcover. The parlour stands a few hundred yards from the Athenaeum where he read as a young man, and from the doorways he copied into his fiction.
sources: Providence city directories, 1937 and 1938, via Open Library full-text search
Nominatim geocode, 187 Benefit Street, College Hill, Providence
suggested_refs: Horace B. Knowles' Sons Inc., 187 Benefit Street, Providence

stops.name: Swan Point Cemetery, Providence: the Phillips plot
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by hplovecraft.com: buried 18 March 1937 in the Phillips family plot. Coordinate reconciled to the Nominatim geocode for Swan Point Cemetery, since the dossier carried two different points for the same grave about a kilometre apart; the exact plot within the grounds is not given in the sources reached.
stops.campa: He is buried in his grandfather's plot on the slope above the Seekonk, under the family monument, his name cut into the Phillips stone with the rest of them and no marker of his own. Whipple Van Buren Phillips is here, and Sarah Susan, and Winfield Scott Lovecraft, brought out of Butler Hospital thirty-nine years before and put in the ground in 1898. The household had run out of money and then out of people. Swan Point lies half a mile from Angell Street, where all of them began.
sources: Nominatim geocode, Swan Point Cemetery, Providence
suggested_refs: The Phillips family monument, Swan Point Cemetery, 585 Blackstone Boulevard

stops.name: John Hay Library, Providence: the papers come to Brown
stops.date_confidence: the gathering is attested to 1937, when Barlow acted on the Instructions in Case of Decease; the donation to the John Hay Library followed later and Wikipedia's article on Barlow gives no year for it, so this stop is dated April 1937 to order the segment and should be read as 'from 1937 onward'. Coordinate is the Nominatim geocode for the John Hay Library, 20-34 Prospect Street.
stops.campa: R. H. Barlow, twenty years old, comes north with a written instruction in his pocket and gathers what there is: manuscripts, letters, amateur papers, photographs, the books. Derleth will dispute his standing for years, but the founding archival act is Barlow's. The collection ends up on Prospect Street at Brown University, a few hundred yards from the College Street room where most of it was written and from the front steps of the university that never admitted him. In what year it reaches the library the record does not say.
sources: Brown University John Hay Library finding aid, riamco.org, US-RPB-mslovecraft
Nominatim geocode, John Hay Library, 20-34 Prospect Street
suggested_refs: The H. P. Lovecraft Collection, John Hay Library, Brown University

stops.name: 65 Prospect Street, Providence: the house moved two blocks north
stops.date_confidence: year attested: The New Annotated H. P. Lovecraft gives 'originally built in 1825 at 66 College Street. In 1959 it was moved to 65 Prospect Street,' and De Camp's biography says the same. Month and day defaulted to 01. The relocation resolves the College Street versus Prospect Street contradiction the dossier had left open. Coordinate is the OSM listing for the Samuel B. Mumford House at its present site.
stops.campa: Brown University wants the lot, and rather than pull down a house of 1825 the university has it lifted off its foundations and carried two blocks north up the hill. The address changes with it: 66 College Street becomes 65 Prospect Street, which is why half the reference books give one number and half the other for the room where he died. He had loved the house for standing where it stood, colonial and permanent. It stands now two blocks north of that.
sources: The New Annotated H. P. Lovecraft, ed. Klinger
L. Sprague de Camp, H. P. Lovecraft: A Biography

stops.name: Swan Point Cemetery, Providence: I AM PROVIDENCE
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Wikipedia; month and day defaulted to 01. The 2015 retirement of the World Fantasy Award trophy cast in his likeness is attested by Wikipedia's World Fantasy Award article and is noted here as a fact about his name, not as a scene at this grave.
stops.campa: Forty years after the burial, readers who never met him pay for a stone of his own and cut into it a line from a letter he wrote to his aunt from Brooklyn. In the same decades the name is argued over rather than simply honored: the fantasy field's chief award was cast in his likeness from 1975, and in 2015 it was retired over the racism his own letters document past any denying. They come to the grave anyway, with flowers, coins, pencils and printed copies of the stories, and the groundskeepers clear the offerings away, and the offerings come back.
stops.quote: That is not dead which can eternal lie, and with strange aeons even death may die.
stops.quote_source: H. P. Lovecraft, The Call of Cthulhu (1926), the Necronomicon couplet quoted by old Castro
